# Closure and Escalation Notes

**Suspicious Process Access to LSASS Memory** · `T1003.001_lsass_memory_access` · [T1003.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/)

Fill in only what you checked. A confirmed attack is never closed from the queue: send the escalation note instead.

## Benign Positive

The rule fired on real activity that is expected and authorized.

```text
Alert:        T1003.001_lsass_memory_access for <host> at <time, UTC>
Observed:     TargetImage=<value>  SourceImage=<value>  GrantedAccess=<value>
Checked:      1. Identify SourceImage, its signer, parent and user -> <result>
              2. Search for a .dmp file written by the same process within 2 minutes (Sysmon EID 11) -> <result>
              3. Check whether SourceImage is a known EDR, AV or backup agent in your environment -> <result>
Benign:       <which known source below> - confirmed by <change record, owner or ticket>
Disposition:  Benign Positive
Tuning:       none | windows_components (applied) | powershell_process_listing (applied) | defender_engine (applied) | edr_agent_by_full_path (proposed) | defender_program_files (proposed) | azure_guest_agent (proposed)
```

Known benign sources for this detection:
- EDR, AV and backup agents that open LSASS for inspection
- Defender running from C:\Program Files\Windows Defender (builds without platform updates) and EDR sensors
- svchost-hosted services, Task Manager, WerFault and the Malicious Software Removal Tool on some builds
- {'PowerShell 7 (pwsh.exe) Get-Process': 'its .NET runtime has no System.ni.dll frame, so the process-listing filter does not apply'}
- VMware Tools, configuration managers (SCCM) and other management agents
- Cloud virtual machine agents (the Azure guest agent's log collector)
- Windows components outside the named list on builds not covered by public data (add them by full path)
- Administrators creating LSASS dumps for a Microsoft support case

Never tune:
- Never allow-list by process name alone (MsMpEng.exe, procdump.exe): a renamed copy in a writable folder would pass.
- Never filter a whole folder such as System32: public data shows a dumper dropped into System32 (nanodump), a fresh services.exe dumping through dbgcore (PPLdump) and rundll32 and Task Manager dumps - all from that folder.
- Never filter PowerShell without the access mask and the .NET frame: Invoke-Mimikatz runs inside powershell.exe.

```text

Risk:         base 60 + <conditions met> = <score>
Preserved:    ProcessAccess event with GrantedAccess and CallTrace -> <where it is saved>
              Process tree of SourceImage -> <where it is saved>
              Any dump file and its hash -> <where it is saved>
              Logon sessions on the host since last reboot -> <where it is saved>
Containment:  none yet | <action taken, time UTC>
Recommended:  Treat as credential theft: isolate the host, reset every credential used on it since boot, hunt for reuse of those accounts
```

Escalate when any of these holds:
1. SourceImage is unsigned, renamed, or in a user-writable path
2. rundll32.exe with comsvcs.dll on the command line
3. Any dump file created near the access
4. Authentication anomalies from the host afterwards (NTLM or logon type 9)

Risk conditions: host is critical +20 · payload in user writable path +15 · user is privileged +10 · known vendor software -30 · approved admin activity -20.

Containment options, after the evidence above is preserved:
1. Isolate the host
2. Reset credentials of every account that logged on to the host since last reboot, including service accounts
3. Hunt for reuse of those credentials across the estate
